Q: How can I retrieve a saved keystore password from Android Studio? A:

Working in 2026 Feb, Android Studio Narwhal 3.
Plugins > Search for Material Theme UI > Install > Restart IDE

After IDE is restarted,
Build > Generate Signed App Bundle or APK.
Click on the password EditText on the same dialog and an eye icon will appear.

Q: how to manipulate history on browser navigation in next js app A:

You can fix that simply by using replace.
What you are using now for your project?

Here are three types solution for JS, React and Next.js.

  1. JS: window.history.replaceState({}, '', '?page=1&limit=50');

  2. React: navigate('?page=1&limit=50', { replace: true });

  3. Next.js:

    router.replace({
  pathname: router.pathname,
  query: { page: 1, limit: 50 },
});

Q: How is the progress percentage in CMake-generated Make builds calculated? A:

They're percentages of progress in performing "progress actions", which appears to include:

  • building object files
  • building libraries
  • building executables
  • custom build rules

From my very cursory look, I think the 100% is distributed uniformly between all progress actions. I wouldn't assume that CMake has visibility into what's done inside a custom command.

If you want to take a look at the guts of the print commands in the generated Makefiles, grep your build directory for "progress-num".

Q: Why does Float'Succ behave differently on Float-variables than on Float-expressions? A:

According to the Barnes book "Ada 2005" Chapter 6.8, Float'Succ will deliver the next implemented number, in Appendix 1.2 called next "machine number". This feature can in fact be interesting when doing unit-testing boundary tests with floating point numbers. In java, for example, there is a similar function called nextUp.

Regarding your question why I wrote Float'Succ(Float(Pi)): I first wrote Float'Succ(Pi) and noticed that it was printed exactly as just Pi. Assuming that Pi might be not of type Float but rather some larger Float type I had tried to cast Pi to Float. But, yes, Float'Succ(Pi) also was unexpectedly identical to Pi.

Put(Float'Succ(Float_Pi), ...) shows the incremented number, which also gave me the impression that Pi might be of a wider Float type.
